entry.title: Why Prompt-Level Controls Are the New Frontier of AI Risk Management
entry.summary: Generative AI risks are no longer limited to models and data. The real vulnerability now lives in prompts. As highlighted by Technology Radius, prompt-level governance is emerging as a critical control point for enterprises adopting AI at scale (source). Prompts are no longer harmless inputs. They are attack surfaces. Prompts determine: What data AI can access How models behave What outputs are generated A poorly written prompt can: Leak confidential data Trigger biased responses Bypass safeguards This makes prompts a governance priority. Most organizations underestimated prompt risk. Sensitive data exposure Jailbreak attempts Policy circumvention Unauthorized task execution These risks scale fast. Especially in enterprise environments. Manual reviews do not work. AI operates too quickly. Real-time prompt inspection Automated policy enforcement Context-aware filtering Logging and traceability Governance must be embedded. Prompt governance touches multiple teams. But ownership must be clear. CIO teams manage tooling and integration CISO teams enforce security rules Compliance teams define restrictions Without coordination, controls break. Prompt governance enables scale. It allows organizations to: Move faster Reduce risk Maintain compliance By 2026, prompt-level controls will be standard. AI governance no longer starts with the model. It starts with the prompt. Organizations that secure prompts secure their AI future.

entry.title: Who Should Lead AI Governance in 2026: CIOs, CISOs, or Ethics Teams?
entry.summary: AI governance is no longer a theoretical discussion. It is now an operational necessity. As generative AI becomes embedded across enterprise systems, the question of ownership has grown urgent. According to insights shared by Technology Radius in its analysis of emerging governance trends, organizations are actively redefining who should lead AI governance efforts (source). The answer is no longer simple. But the direction is clear. Traditionally, AI governance lived with ethics committees and legal teams. Their role focused on principles, not execution. Responsible AI guidelines Bias and fairness standards Policy documentation Regulatory interpretation This worked when AI use was limited. It does not work at scale. Generative AI systems now: Handle sensitive enterprise data Influence decisions Operate continuously Ethics teams rarely control infrastructure or deployment. Without enforcement power, governance becomes symbolic. Symbolic governance creates risk. CIOs are stepping into governance because AI runs on enterprise platforms. They manage: Cloud environments AI tool integration Development pipelines Governance can be embedded into system design Policies become technical controls Risk is addressed early This shifts governance from theory to execution. AI introduces new security threats. Prompt injection. Data leakage. Model misuse. These are security problems. Risk assessment frameworks Continuous monitoring Access control enforcement Incident response In 2026, AI risk equals security risk. The strongest organizations define clear roles. A practical structure CIO→ Platform and lifecycle governance CISO→ Security and risk enforcement Ethics & Legal → Policy and regulatory guidance Governance works when authority matches responsibility. AI governance is no longer a document. It is an operating system. Organizations that understand this will scale AI safely. Those that don’t will fall behind.
